divination.statement: How can he stand by his decision to use parliamentary urgency to push through legislation that will increase unemployment and insecure working conditions, while reducing wages, when people are trying to survive a cost of living crisis and put more kai on the table for Christmas?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government's urgency employment legislation (90-day trials, Fair Pay Agreement repeal) will raise unemployment and insecure work and reduce wages. Not a promise about her own action, so it is a prediction rather than a commitment.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate and QES average hourly earnings (real terms) for the two years following December 2023, plus the temporary/insecure employment measure; true if unemployment rises materially and real wages fall over that window, false if unemployment is flat or falling and real wages hold or rise.

divination.statement: So those pricings should go down.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that petrol prices will fall following the removal of the fuel charging imposed by the previous Government (the Auckland regional fuel tax). This is an outcome in the market, not a promise about the Government's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly retail petrol price data for Auckland before and after the repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax; true if Auckland pump prices fall by broadly the amount of the removed levy (about 11.5c/litre) net of international price movements, false if prices do not fall or rise.

focus.statement: But it’s been my observation that the Greens—the economies that they admire are all in the Third World.
focus.explanation: Answering a question about wages and employment law, but this sentence names no policy, measure, figure or outcome. It is entirely a characterisation of what the other party is 'really like'. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched — this is exactly the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: At the end of the last three years, the workers of this country were dramatically let down by a failed economy, and our job is to turn that around.
focus.explanation: Directed at the previous Government's record in general terms — 'a failed economy' — with no named policy, measure, figure or outcome. Scrutiny of a predecessor is legitimate and would score high if a specific commitment or number were named; here nothing is, so most of the weight is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, you are going to hold us to that—you won’t have to hold us to that because unlike that member, we keep our promises. We don’t just make them and break them one after the other; we keep them.
focus.explanation: Prompted by a question on fuel and food costs, but the content is entirely about the other side's character as promise-breakers. No policy, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, first of all, the integrity of the person answering this question on the subject of incomes and wages is that that threshold was set in the previous Government, not by Labour or the Greens but by New Zealand First.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the minimum wage level in force was set during the 2017–2020 Government by New Zealand First rather than by Labour or the Greens — a claim about which party authored the policy, not about the wage figure itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2017 Labour–New Zealand First coalition agreement and the Cabinet papers/Budget decisions on minimum wage increases 2017–2020; true if the minimum wage path was a New Zealand First-negotiated provision, false if it was a Labour manifesto commitment carried by Labour Ministers.

veracity.statement: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms’ overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms' overall hiring, and that they reduced dismissal costs. The claim is about the content of a specific study's findings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2016 Treasury-commissioned study on the 90-day trial period (Chappell & Sin, Motu, Treasury working paper); true if it reports no statistically significant increase in overall hiring attributable to trial periods, false if it reports a significant positive hiring effect.

veracity.statement: That is the purpose and the focus of this Government—that with the reforms that are going to go ahead, running a far more successful economy, and ensuring that no one is left out in housing, education, and health, and in terms of infrastructure access, then people will be uplifted; not like the disaster we had, where there were all those tens and tens and tens of thousands utterly forgotten, and the homeless went up by 35 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that homelessness increased by 35 percent under the previous Government. A specific percentage change in a measured quantity over a stated period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates and MHUD emergency/transitional housing and public housing register data between 2017 and 2023; true if the relevant homelessness measure rose by approximately 35 percent over that period, false if the change is materially different or no measure supports the figure.

veracity.statement: And whilst I’m at it, they left this country’s fuel supply in a desperate circumstance when they wound back Marsden Point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government wound back the Marsden Point refinery and thereby left New Zealand's fuel supply in a desperate state. The checkable core is who made the decision to end refining and what happened to fuel security stockholding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2021 Refining NZ (Channel Infrastructure) shareholder decision record and the previous Government's fuel security policy and minimum stockholding obligation; true if the conversion to an import terminal was a Government decision or one it declined to prevent while leaving reserves reduced, false if it was a commercial decision by the company's shareholders and stockholding requirements were maintained or increased.

veracity.statement: I’m advised that the 1:480 ratio was never finalised, nor was it funded adequately by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things about the previous Government: that the 1:480 police-to-population ratio was never finalised as a commitment, and that it was not adequately funded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet papers, coalition agreements and Budget appropriations 2017–2023 relating to the 1:480 police-to-population ratio; true if no formal decision adopted the ratio and no appropriation was made to sustain it, false if Cabinet or Budget documents record it as an adopted and funded target.

veracity.statement: They delivered 1,800 additional police officers, and they’re now committed to an additional 500.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand First delivered 1,800 additional police officers during the 2017–2020 term. The checkable core is whether constabulary numbers actually rose by that amount over that period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Police constabulary FTE workforce data for October 2017 to late 2020 against the 1,800 new officers commitment in the 2017 coalition agreement; true if net constabulary numbers rose by approximately 1,800 over that term, false if the net increase falls materially short.

specificity.statement: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms’ overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
specificity.explanation: Names the measure (90-day trial periods), the affected group, and cites a dated, identifiable piece of commissioned research with its finding. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we’re going to help all those people who are working with the poor, then the first thing we should do is uplift our economy, and leave no one out.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the answer to a question about policies for child poverty, but commits to nothing checkable: no measure, no figure, no timeframe, no mechanism. 'Uplift our economy' and 'leave no one out' are directional slogans.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And on the bigger question of costs of living before Christmas, well there’s only two weeks to go and we’re going to do the best we can to signal to the market and through the Groceries Commissioner a fairer pricing regime going forward.
specificity.explanation: Names one real instrument — the Groceries Commissioner — but supplies no mechanism, no amount and no date beyond 'going forward'. 'Signal to the market' and 'do the best we can' commit to nothing that could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the number of constabulary fulltime-equivalents be 500 higher in two years’ time?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: a named measure (constabulary FTE), a figure (500) and a timeframe (two years). Anyone could go and verify the answer later.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The fact is—if anyone understands economics—a willing business and a willing worker are critical to employment. So whether it’s one month, two months, or three months, the fact of the matter is that the sound connection of those two will work.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: that employment requires a willing employer and a willing employee says nothing about whether the length of a trial period changes hiring or dismissal outcomes. The conclusion ('whether it's one month, two months, or three months... will work') does not follow from the premise, and the cited Treasury finding it was offered against is not engaged. The prefatory 'if anyone understands economics' is an appeal to expertise standing in for the argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: On the marae, Megan, you keep quiet. You do. Willie knows that; he keeps quiet too. You don’t shout out like some bunch of clowns at university.
civility.explanation: Turns on named individual members, addressing one by first name and instructing her to be quiet, and likens their conduct to 'some bunch of clowns'. Nothing here engages the substance of the question about the cost of living; it is directed at the people.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just following on from the speaker who has resumed his seat, the reality is that there was a slight delay in the translation, reflective of the rudimentary nature of the Māori language and my ability to make it sound more sophisticated in English.
civility.explanation: Raised under a point of order but the content is not procedural: it disparages te reo Māori as 'rudimentary' while claiming personal credit for sophistication, mocking the member who had just asked his question in that language. Sneering directed at a colleague's contribution rather than at any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, you are going to hold us to that—you won’t have to hold us to that because unlike that member, we keep our promises. We don’t just make them and break them one after the other; we keep them.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named individual member — that he makes promises intending to break them 'one after the other'. Short of a direct insult, but it is a charge against the person rather than against a policy or an argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We could be closed down within three days because of their short-sightedness, and Megan Woods is the person who never acted in international interests—just allowed the refinery that is so critical to this country in an emergency to be not operating any longer.
civility.explanation: Names a specific member and charges her personally with never having acted in the country's interests. That goes past criticising a decision she made — brutal criticism of the Marsden Point decision itself would score high here — and becomes a claim about her disposition as a Minister.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When order becomes disorder, grandparents stop going out for grocery shopping, parents don’t let their kids walk home from school, and dairy owners have to serve people from within cages. Our police should always be given the powers and resources they need to do the job they do best: keeping us safe.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to emotion via vivid imagery. The premises describe fear of disorder; the conclusion is about police powers and resources. Nothing offered connects the two — no evidence that additional police powers or resources address the described behaviours. The inference is left entirely implicit.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Social investment in housing: when I worked at Te Mahia Community Village, a transitional housing facility in Takanini, I saw the significant drop in antisocial behaviour when social wraparound services are partnered with housing providers.
rigor.explanation: Generalisation from a single personal anecdote. One observed site is offered as support for a general policy claim about wraparound services, with no comparison group, no measure of the 'significant drop', and no account of what else changed at that facility. The premise is a real observation, which lifts it above a bare appeal, but the conclusion outruns it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While I strongly commend the traditional school systems, I also place merit in alternative school programmes and alternative education programmes and charter schools, because not every child learns the same way.
rigor.explanation: The premise — children learn differently — genuinely supports a case for varied provision, so the inference is not empty. But it underdetermines the conclusion: it gives no reason to prefer charter schools specifically over other forms of differentiated provision within the state system. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Social investment in our youth to help build their mental resilience and protect them from the lure of gangs; social investment to combat youth crime, where positive mentors teach our troubled youth self-discipline.
specificity.explanation: Names a policy framework (social investment) and one mechanism (mentoring), but carries no figures, no funding, no delivery agency and no timeframe. A reader could not check or act on it. It sits above a pure slogan only because mentoring is a nameable intervention.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Takanini is enriched, with over 50 percent of its residents born overseas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority of residents of the Takanini electorate were born outside New Zealand. The claim is about the electorate's population as at the statement date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census birthplace data for the Takanini general electorate (or the 2018 figures on the notional boundary): true if the overseas-born share exceeds 50 percent, false if it is 50 percent or below.

veracity.statement: You ran the campaign the way you wanted, and in Takanini, I’m proud that we achieved the highest swing of the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Takanini recorded the largest swing of any electorate in the 2023 general election. Takanini was a new seat, so any swing is measured against notional 2020 results on the redrawn boundary; the claim is presumably about the swing to National.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 electorate results compared with the Representation Commission's notional 2020 results on the 2023 boundaries: true if Takanini shows the largest swing to National (candidate or party vote) of any electorate, false if any other electorate exceeds it.

civility.statement: And that is dishonest, because you can’t do them all—the advice says so.
civility.explanation: Labels the opposing party's campaign position "dishonest", imputing bad faith rather than confining the criticism to the incompatibility of the commitments. Short of a personal insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They told the electorate they would do one thing, and now they’ve done another and they’re patting themselves on the back—I think it’s disgraceful.
civility.explanation: Aimed at the Government's conduct rather than any individual's character, but "patting themselves on the back" and "disgraceful" are sneering in tone, edging past robust criticism of the decision itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Prime Minister fronts up on any topic and on any question and he does so, on most parts, with a smile, although the smile’s not as wide as it once was these days, I might say.
civility.explanation: Opens with genuine credit, then lands a personal dig at the Prime Minister's demeanour rather than at any argument or decision. Mild as jibes go, but it is about the man, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And that is dishonest, because you can’t do them all—the advice says so.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — the four campaign commitments cannot all be met — but the support offered is a bare appeal to unnamed "advice". No mechanism or figure is given to show why they are mutually exclusive.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This makes it easier for the Government to pay for their tax cuts because they don’t have to continue to support councils to go along with this reform process.
rigor.explanation: The fiscal step is sound in itself — money not spent supporting councils is money available elsewhere — but the conclusion that this is what funds the tax cuts is asserted, not shown; no figure links the foregone council support to the tax package. A gap between what was offered and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There will be councils that want to join with others but can’t because those others don’t want to, because why on earth would they voluntarily agree to sign up to take on the debt and the burden that the other council brings?
rigor.explanation: A genuine incentive argument: under a voluntary scheme, a low-debt council has no reason to absorb a high-debt neighbour's liabilities, so some councils will be unable to find partners. The inference tracks, though it is put as a rhetorical question rather than evidenced with any council's position.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have been asking the National Party to provide numbers to back up their claims right from when they first announced this policy 12 months ago and they have refused every single time, and now they’re in Government and they’re refusing again because they know it doesn’t stack up.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a refusal to release costings to a specific inner belief that the costings fail — an argument from absence of evidence combined with mind-reading. Non-disclosure has many explanations; nothing offered rules the others out.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Their own advice says so: the Department of Internal Affairs has on their own website, even today, advice that criticises the analysis that the Government has based their policy decisions on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that material published on the Department of Internal Affairs website as at 13 February 2024 criticises the analysis underpinning the Government's Local Water Done Well policy decisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA published advice/regulatory impact material on water services reform available on dia.govt.nz in February 2024 (including archived Wayback captures); true if any such document critiques the analysis the Government relied on for its repeal/replacement policy, false if no such published critique existed on that site.

veracity.statement: When the Minister, on Morning Report today, declared that this will be cheaper, he didn’t say it will be cheaper for ratepayers; he said it will be cheaper for them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Minister of Local Government said in a specific RNZ Morning Report interview on 13 February 2024 — that the claimed saving was framed as cheaper for the Government rather than for ratepayers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RNZ Morning Report audio/transcript of 13 February 2024 featuring the Minister of Local Government; true if the Minister's cost claim is framed as a saving to the Crown/Government without saying ratepayers, false if he attributed the saving to ratepayers.

veracity.statement: Now, I live in Wairarapa, and in South Wairarapa that council has had no choice but to increase rates by 20 percent for two years in a row, and that doesn’t account for water services.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that South Wairarapa District Council raised rates by about 20 percent in each of two consecutive years, and that those increases exclude water services costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: South Wairarapa District Council annual plans / long-term plan rates resolutions for the two rating years preceding February 2024; true if the average rates increase was approximately 20% in each of two consecutive years, false if materially lower or if only one year reached that level.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister today was asked by Newshub about his numbers to justify their predictions. He walked away.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on 13 February 2024 the Prime Minister was questioned by Newshub about the figures underpinning the Government's water reform claims and declined to answer, physically leaving the interview.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Newshub footage and reporting from 13 February 2024 of the Prime Minister being questioned about water reform costings; true if he ends the exchange and walks off without answering, false if he answered the question or no such exchange occurred.

veracity.statement: What they are repealing, and what the members of the National, ACT, and New Zealand First parties are about to vote to do, is repeal the affordable water reforms—the reforms that the Government’s own advice shows would save ratepayers thousands a year by 2051.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice held by the Government projects savings to ratepayers of thousands of dollars a year by 2051 under the affordable water reforms being repealed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The DIA-commissioned modelling underpinning the Affordable Water Reforms (the Water Industry Commission for Scotland analysis and DIA cost projections); true if it projects annual per-household water charges under the reforms thousands of dollars lower than the status quo by 2051, false if no such projection exists or the projected gap is materially smaller.

specificity.statement: Their own advice says so: the Department of Internal Affairs has on their own website, even today, advice that criticises the analysis that the Government has based their policy decisions on.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (DIA), the medium (its website) and the timeframe ("even today"), so a listener could go and look — but does not name the document, the analysis criticised, or what the criticism says.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, I live in Wairarapa, and in South Wairarapa that council has had no choice but to increase rates by 20 percent for two years in a row, and that doesn’t account for water services.
specificity.explanation: Names the council, the size of the increase and the number of years, and flags what the figure excludes. Directly checkable against that council's rating documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What they are repealing, and what the members of the National, ACT, and New Zealand First parties are about to vote to do, is repeal the affordable water reforms—the reforms that the Government’s own advice shows would save ratepayers thousands a year by 2051.
specificity.explanation: Names the legislation being repealed, the parties voting for it, the source of the estimate, the magnitude and the horizon. Someone could go to the modelling and check the number.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It is not unfeasible to say that there will be some councils that go bankrupt without a financial guarantee that this Government promised them when they were campaigning.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, absent a central-government financial guarantee, one or more New Zealand councils will become insolvent. Hedged ("not unfeasible"), but the forecast event is a discrete, observable one.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Local Government Commission records and council annual reports; true if at least one territorial authority becomes insolvent, defaults, or has a Crown Manager/Commission appointed on grounds of financial failure attributable to water services costs, false if no council reaches insolvency or Crown financial intervention in that period.

focus.statement: There will be councils that want to join with others but can’t because those others don’t want to, because why on earth would they voluntarily agree to sign up to take on the debt and the burden that the other council brings?
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the mechanism of the replacement policy — voluntary council amalgamation of water services — and who it leaves stranded. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s still there, but they’re removing the access for people who cannot afford it.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it names what the bill does and does not do to section 27 reports (retains the ability, removes the funded access). No party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So do not sit in this House and yell at us about who cares for victims, because removing the funding for these reports is not caring about victims.
focus.explanation: Directed at the named measure — the removal of funding for the reports — rather than at the other party's general character, even though it is delivered as a rebuke.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s still there, but they’re removing the access for people who cannot afford it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill leaves the section 27 report mechanism available but withdraws the legal aid funding that lets those who cannot pay use it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Legal Services Amendment Bill as introduced/reported back, read against s27 of the Sentencing Act 2002 and the legal aid schedules: true if the amendment removes legal aid funding for cultural/s27 reports while leaving intact the offender's ability to have such information put before the court; false if the ability itself is also removed, or if legal aid funding for these reports is retained.

veracity.statement: The problem as we see it is quite clear: in 2017, section 27 reports were costing $40,000; last financial year, $7.7 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific growth in legal-aid-funded expenditure on section 27 reports, from about $40,000 in 2017 to about $7.7 million in the most recent financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / legal aid expenditure figures for section 27 (cultural) reports: true if spending was approximately $40,000 in 2016/17 and approximately $7.7 million in 2022/23, false if either figure is materially different from the published expenditure for the year referred to.

rigor.statement: Not once, in three years of sitting with victims, as a Minister, have I heard them ask to remove these cultural reports.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal anecdote combined with an argument from absence: her own unrecorded experience of meetings is offered as evidence about what victims as a class want. Nothing connects the sample she met to victims generally.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the things—again, the members can go and read in Chief Victims Adviser reports that this current adversarial justice approach actually ends up harming victims more, because, by its nature, it requires a winner and a loser.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a stated mechanism (an adversarial process necessarily produces losers, and victims are among them) and a named source. The gap is that nothing links this general critique to the funding change actually at issue, so the conclusion is broader than the support offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They have written across social media and across media, and they have been very clear: all that removing the funding for cultural reports will do is entrench further discrimination in a justice system that already is trying to resolve its own discrimination.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the conclusion rests entirely on unnamed frontline workers having 'been very clear', with no mechanism or evidence offered for how removing the funding entrenches discrimination.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know the power, in my very short time at the criminal bar, of actually having an employer turn up and speak on behalf of an offender and actually talk about how they can help that person actually stop their reoffending.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: a self-described 'very short time' at the criminal bar is offered as the basis for concluding that unfunded personal testimony can substitute for funded reports across the system.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can assure the House that I have held the victims after being raped, I have nursed the children who have been beaten, I have looked into the victim’s eyes, and I have retained a faith in the judiciary and the justice system to act appropriately.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal experience and emotion. The recital of what she has witnessed establishes standing to speak, not a reason why the judiciary will act appropriately; the conclusion does not follow from the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is the judiciary who will weigh up the value of the information presented to them and they will know the difference between a well-coiled-up report written by professionals using special-speak and those impassioned pleas that are given by those who have genuine concern and connection to the offenders and want to see the very best outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to authority: judges are asserted to be able to discriminate between report types, with nothing offered in support, and the contrast between 'special-speak' reports and 'impassioned pleas' is assumed rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Shame on them for trying to exploit rape—because using this racist legislation is trying to exploit rape and sexual violence.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith of a serious kind — that the other side is deliberately exploiting rape and sexual violence for legislative advantage — rather than contesting the effect of the bill. No individual is insulted, which keeps it above the personal-attack band.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge the passion from other members of the House, but we do have a different response to how we want to deal with criminal justice in New Zealand, and we see this as a part of an overall plan that our parties have put together to deal with it.
civility.explanation: Follows a fierce speech and had ample opportunity to answer in kind; instead acknowledges the opposing member's passion and frames the disagreement as one of approach. Attacks nobody.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is for that reason that we do not need taxpayer funding to milk the system, as has been occurring, but we do need the recognition of true, concerned community members to advocate for those who need it at the time of sentencing to represent their concerns.
civility.explanation: 'Milk the system, as has been occurring' imputes bad faith to the people preparing these reports, and 'true, concerned' implies the professionals are not genuine. Short of a personal insult, but no longer engaging only the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The problem as we see it is quite clear: in 2017, section 27 reports were costing $40,000; last financial year, $7.7 million.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures for a named spending line — anyone could go and check the legal aid expenditure on section 27 reports for those years.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because it was recognised that smoking and cigarettes were harmful, we moved towards an environment which was less and less smoky and, actually, fun fact, it wasn’t until 2016—2016—that the entire premises of Parliament finally became entirely smoke-free, including our lawn.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a datable fact: that Parliament's entire premises, including the lawn, only became fully smoke-free in 2016.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Service / Speaker's Office records of the smokefree policy covering the parliamentary precinct; true if the whole precinct including grounds became smoke-free in 2016, false if that took effect in a materially different year.

veracity.statement: So not only are we left in this kind of haze as to why the Government’s progressing this through, because the only entities that we saw advocating for the repeal of this smoke-free generation legislation throughout the past year or so were New Zealand First and the tobacco industry, but who benefits?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the only public advocates for repealing the smokefree generation measures over roughly the preceding year were New Zealand First and the tobacco industry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public advocacy record for repeal of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) legislation from roughly early 2023 to February 2024 — party policy documents, media statements, submissions; true if only NZ First and tobacco companies are found, false if other organisations (e.g. retailer or dairy-owner groups, ACT) publicly advocated repeal.

veracity.statement: There’s actually no cost-benefit analysis that sits alongside this legislation, I might add, which again leaves us with the question of why this is occurring under the urgency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no cost-benefit analysis accompanied the repeal bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whether a regulatory impact statement or cost-benefit analysis was published alongside the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill by the Ministry of Health/Treasury; true if none exists, false if one was published with the bill.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen it drop significantly over the past 12 years, from around 16 percent down to 8.6 percent last year, to 6.8 percent this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts daily smoking prevalence fell from about 16 percent twelve years ago to 8.6 percent and then 6.8 percent in the two most recent years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for 2011/12, 2021/22 and 2022/23; true if the figures match ~16%, 8.6% and 6.8% within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’d like to note that Action for Smokefree 2025 has said that the progress we’re making is unprecedented.
veracity.explanation: Relays a characterisation attributed to ASH New Zealand — that the current rate of progress on smoking reduction is unprecedented.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: ASH New Zealand's published statements and media releases up to February 2024; true if ASH described the recent decline in smoking rates as unprecedented, false if no such statement exists or if their statements characterise the Government's direction otherwise.

veracity.statement: Look, no regulations or programmes that were in place before the election have been stopped.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that nothing already in place before the 2023 election — regulations or programmes — has been discontinued by the Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The status of smokefree measures enacted before October 2023 (denicotinisation requirements, retailer-number reduction, the smokefree generation provision) and of Ministry of Health smoking cessation programmes; true if all remain operative, false if any enacted regulation or funded programme has been repealed or discontinued.

specificity.statement: Well, it’s not the more New Zealanders who are going to be addicted for longer only filling up this Government’s coffers by an approximate $500 million per annum as a result of increased excise in tobacco tax; it’s going to be the tobacco industry.
specificity.explanation: Carries a quantified fiscal figure ($500 million per annum) tied to a named mechanism (tobacco excise revenue), which someone could check — though the sentence is loosely constructed and the timeframe is left open.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve seen it drop significantly over the past 12 years, from around 16 percent down to 8.6 percent last year, to 6.8 percent this year.
specificity.explanation: Three dated prevalence figures and a stated period; directly checkable against the published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There’s actually no cost-benefit analysis that sits alongside this legislation, I might add, which again leaves us with the question of why this is occurring under the urgency.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — a named missing analytical document and the process being used to pass the bill. No party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are ripping off the band-aid really, really quickly in the hopes that this is swept under the rug amongst all of the other heinous things that they are doing under urgency and super-quickly with hopes that, into the future, New Zealanders forget it.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the Government's supposed motives and character — embarrassment, concealment, 'heinous things' in general. No policy, figure or named outcome once the imputation of motive is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We haven’t heard the Opposition give an intelligent reckoning with a second and third order of facts of prohibition of cigarettes on an emerging black market.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point in here — the black-market consequences of restricting cigarette supply — but it is delivered as a characterisation of the Opposition's competence rather than as an engagement with the mechanism itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are not going to take the punitive regulatory approach that the Opposition would like us to do; we’re going to build on what has worked—what has continued to drive down smoking rates.
focus.explanation: A real policy contrast — regulatory restriction versus continuing existing cessation measures — but it is stated through a characterisation of what the Opposition wants rather than by naming the mechanisms on either side.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But to contextualise that in the long run, outside of the three-yearly cycle, we know that this is going to cost us billions of dollars, and therefore it sits in entire contravention to the National Party’s proposals of social investment.
rigor.explanation: The inference is coherent — if long-run health costs run to billions, that does cut against a spend-now-to-save-later social investment framing — but the load-bearing premise is introduced as a bare assertion ('we know'), with no source or modelling offered, leaving a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that kind of begs the question of whether they believe that authoritarian rule is “all g” simply because every three years we have a general election.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the Government's stated position — that an electoral mandate justifies using urgency — is restated as a belief in authoritarian rule, a conclusion the premise does not support. Nothing is offered to bridge 'uses urgency after winning an election' to 'thinks authoritarian rule is acceptable'.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: On the way we’re going, we will reach our goal of having the average under 5 percent by 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that national adult smoking prevalence will fall below the Smokefree 2025 threshold of 5 percent by 2025 — an outcome in the world, not merely an action the speaker controls.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2025 reporting year; true if below 5.0 percent, false if 5.0 percent or above.

rigor.statement: I am disappointed to hear that the rationale for not looking at sections 65C and 65J is because of the campaign approach, whereas it appears—unless the Minister advises the committee otherwise—that the same outcome for Aucklanders could none the less have been achieved by engaging those two sections of the Land Transport Management Act.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: because ss 65C and 65J would deliver the same outcome, the Minister's stated rationale is inadequate. The conclusion tracks the premise, but the premise that those sections could achieve the same result is asserted rather than demonstrated — a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s all very sensible—when you’re changing the law and you’re transitioning to a new system, this is all about making sure that there is accuracy in terms of the amounts which have been received, making sure that they are dispersed, and making sure that any people who are entitled to rebates are still able to receive them.
rigor.explanation: An argument with a stated conclusion (the provisions are sensible) and reasons (accuracy of amounts, disbursal, continuing rebate entitlements during a wind-down). The reasons name genuine purposes a transitional regime must serve, but the step from 'these are the purposes' to 'these clauses achieve them' is asserted, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the question around passing on costs, there is a range of regulatory powers that MBIE have in terms of making sure that happens, and it’s very similar to what happened when the last Government reduced the fuel excise—those expectations remain.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that savings will be passed on — rests on an unspecified appeal to MBIE's 'regulatory powers' and an argument from analogy to the previous excise cut. Neither establishes that pass-through will occur; the analogy also assumes, rather than shows, that the earlier cut was passed through.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Are we, in fact, passing on costs that would otherwise not have been borne by people like my 90-year-old father who drives his car very little but needs to register it every year, and subsidising those people like me who drive great distances because of their work and to get around Auckland?
rigor.explanation: The incidence inference is valid: swapping a per-litre tax for a flat annual registration fee shifts cost from high-mileage to low-mileage drivers, so the redistribution she describes follows from the change she describes. It is carried by two anecdotes used as illustration rather than by distributional data, which is why it falls short of the top.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am disappointed to hear that the rationale for not looking at sections 65C and 65J is because of the campaign approach, whereas it appears—unless the Minister advises the committee otherwise—that the same outcome for Aucklanders could none the less have been achieved by engaging those two sections of the Land Transport Management Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific statutory provisions (ss 65C and 65J of the Land Transport Management Act) and the alternative mechanism. Someone could go to the Act and check whether those sections would do the job.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I invite the—well, I’m interested in the Minister’s response, and my question to the Minister is whether he still stands by the cost of living argument when the departmental disclosure statement very clearly indicates that in some cases, motorists will be around $1.87 better off a week, and the real difference that that would actually make to entertain the cost of living pressures.
specificity.explanation: A named source (the departmental disclosure statement), a precise figure ($1.87) and a stated period (a week). Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So in relation to the nature of the information, obviously there’s archival use, but what’s happening there—and whether there’s actually a requirement, once that information is filed, that that can be disposed of, or whether there is a requirement for that to be retained, as in other parts of the parent Act, where there is a requirement to retain some information for, I think, four years, or thereabouts.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete gap — record retention versus disposal after the scheme ends — and anchors it to a comparable retention period elsewhere in the parent Act. Detail is real but hedged ('I think, four years, or thereabouts') and the clause reference is left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the agency’s advice, in clause 18, all the advice that the New Zealand Transport Agency is required to provide the Minister currently, continues to be provided as the scheme is wound down. That relates to collection, auditing, administrating rebates, transferring net revenue, and monitoring revenue, cost, fuel prices, and volumes.
specificity.explanation: Answers with the named clause and an itemised list of the advice functions that carry over — collection, auditing, rebates, net revenue transfer, monitoring of prices and volumes. Concrete enough to check against the clause, though no frequency is given despite that being asked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There will be 10c plus the corresponding 1.5c a litre in GST that will be reduced from people’s fuel bills; they’ll benefit through this saving.
specificity.explanation: Gives the exact per-litre amounts (10c plus 1.5c GST) and where the saving lands. Precise and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the question around passing on costs, there is a range of regulatory powers that MBIE have in terms of making sure that happens, and it’s very similar to what happened when the last Government reduced the fuel excise—those expectations remain.
specificity.explanation: Asked precisely how pass-through would be assured, the answer offers 'a range of regulatory powers' without naming a power, an instrument, a monitoring mechanism or a consequence for non-compliance. The one concrete anchor is a reference to the earlier excise reduction.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just to give the Minister a minute to consider my question, I will ask the second one, which is: who will benefit from those savings the most? And that should be read in the context of replacing some of the costs that were raised by the Government from the Auckland fuel tax with the $50 fee increase in drivers’ registrations of their vehicles.
specificity.explanation: Names both mechanisms being traded off (the Auckland regional fuel tax and the $50 registration fee increase) and gives the figure for the offsetting charge. The question itself — who benefits most — is left open rather than quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This relates to the Minister’s own electorate, and I do think that the committee does deserve a response around the perception of conflicts of interest, given that the Minister is the member for Pakuranga and this is a project that would obviously be of huge benefit at the expense of other Aucklanders if this was to proceed.
civility.explanation: Raises a perceived conflict of interest, which edges onto the Minister's personal motives rather than the merits of the project. It is hedged as a 'perception' and framed as a question the committee is owed, so it stops short of imputing outright bad faith, but it is more than criticism of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This goes back a long time, when Trevor Mallard was Minister of Education—so I’m afraid, Minister, this might have been before you were born, or perhaps not; it’s hard to tell.
civility.explanation: A personal remark about the Minister's youth rather than anything he has argued. It is light and good-humoured rather than contemptuous, but it is aimed at the man, not the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This relates to the Minister’s own electorate, and I do think that the committee does deserve a response around the perception of conflicts of interest, given that the Minister is the member for Pakuranga and this is a project that would obviously be of huge benefit at the expense of other Aucklanders if this was to proceed.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project (Project 4) in a specific order and the specific ground of objection (benefit to one electorate at the expense of other Aucklanders). This is scrutiny of an identified measure, not content-free party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, in my earlier contribution today, I’d indicated that I’d had a look at what one could get for $1.87 at a supermarket in Auckland, and what you could get is a 227-gram tin of chunky pineapple.
focus.explanation: Engages the government's own stated justification for the bill — cost of living relief — by testing the size of the claimed saving. It is about the measure's effect, not about the other party's character, though the illustration is rhetorical rather than analytical.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Are we, in fact, passing on costs that would otherwise not have been borne by people like my 90-year-old father who drives his car very little but needs to register it every year, and subsidising those people like me who drive great distances because of their work and to get around Auckland?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the measure — who bears the cost and who receives the benefit once the fuel tax is replaced by a registration fee increase. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I invite the—well, I’m interested in the Minister’s response, and my question to the Minister is whether he still stands by the cost of living argument when the departmental disclosure statement very clearly indicates that in some cases, motorists will be around $1.87 better off a week, and the real difference that that would actually make to entertain the cost of living pressures.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an official departmental disclosure statement puts the weekly saving to some motorists at around $1.87. The claim is about what a named published document says, not about whether the saving is adequate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill: true if it states a saving of approximately $1.87 per week for motorists in some cases, false if the stated figure is materially different or no such per-week figure appears.

veracity.statement: There are 14 projects that are suggested to be either retained or dispensed with under this bill, and each in their own right is going to have a huge impact either way on the communities in Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of projects dealt with by the bill. Only the count is checkable; the accompanying characterisation of impact is not operationalised.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedule of projects in the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill as introduced: true if 14 projects are listed to be retained or discontinued, false if the bill lists a materially different number. (The 'huge impact' clause is not part of the checkable claim.)

divination.statement: So it’s all very sensible stuff, which I’m sure the Opposition is very happy to support.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Opposition will support the bill. Recorded as a prediction about how other parties will vote, not as a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the next reading of the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill: true if the opposition parties voted in favour, false if Labour or other opposition parties voted against.

divination.statement: There will be 10c plus the corresponding 1.5c a litre in GST that will be reduced from people’s fuel bills; they’ll benefit through this saving.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the full 10c tax plus 1.5c GST will come off retail fuel bills. Pass-through depends on the conduct of fuel companies, so this is a prediction about an outcome in the world rather than a promise about the Minister's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly retail fuel price monitoring for Auckland versus the rest of New Zealand in the months following the end of the regional fuel tax: true if the Auckland price differential falls by approximately 11.5c per litre, false if the observed reduction is materially smaller (i.e. the cut is not passed through at the pump).

civility.statement: However, we do not believe that this specific piece of legislation is the right way forward.
civility.explanation: A contested bill with a real opportunity to disparage its sponsor — instead she rejects the legislation itself and attacks nobody. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I will hold this Minister to account when he says that he does not think fees should be charged for Companies Office changes which are about safety.
civility.explanation: A pointed challenge to a Minister she disagrees with, aimed entirely at a stated position on fees rather than at him. Robust scrutiny, no imputation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So you could use that website to find out who those directors were and who those shareholders were, and hold them to account.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism at issue — what the public register does and why the address information is there. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You know, we don’t want to see people using it as a tool to evade theft or fraud.
focus.explanation: Engages the substantive objection to the measure — that address suppression could shield wrongdoers — rather than the sponsoring party. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They can use things that already enjoy the protections of limited liability, but still allow directors to not have their addresses published—things like limited partnerships which allow them to have all of their address details withheld from public view.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the legal mechanism — which entity types already permit address suppression and which do not. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If Labour and ACT can agree, surely we can agree that this is, indeed, sticking up for the little guy.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point (the bill helps small operators) but the weight of the sentence is party arithmetic rather than the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I hope members in all parties can listen to this debate and change their minds here and now, because there is nothing in this bill which would create harm, there is nothing in this bill which would put the directors in a worse position than they were before, and there’s certainly nothing in this bill that would put shareholders in a worse position than they were before.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the contents and effects of the bill before the House — directors, shareholders, harm. No party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I will hold this Minister to account when he says that he does not think fees should be charged for Companies Office changes which are about safety.
focus.explanation: Names the specific commitment (no fees for safety-related Companies Office changes) she intends to hold him to. Accountability against a named undertaking, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So you could use that website to find out who those directors were and who those shareholders were, and hold them to account.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism (the Companies Office register, directors and shareholders) and the use it is put to, but carries no figures, thresholds or provisions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: You know, we don’t want to see people using it as a tool to evade theft or fraud.
specificity.explanation: Names a category of harm but no mechanism, no threshold and no example of how suppression would enable evasion. A direction with almost no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They can use things that already enjoy the protections of limited liability, but still allow directors to not have their addresses published—things like limited partnerships which allow them to have all of their address details withheld from public view.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific legal structure (limited partnerships), the specific protection (limited liability) and the specific disclosure difference. Someone could go and check it against the statute.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because myself, I’m actually quite familiar with that process because I was a former journalist, actually, working here in Wellington for TV One News.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about her own employment history: that she worked as a journalist in Wellington for TV One News before entering Parliament. Offered to establish her familiarity with the Companies Office register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Catherine Wedd's published parliamentary biography and TVNZ/One News broadcast credits; true if she was employed as a journalist by TVNZ's One News in Wellington, false if her media career was at a different outlet or in a different role.

veracity.statement: They can use things that already enjoy the protections of limited liability, but still allow directors to not have their addresses published—things like limited partnerships which allow them to have all of their address details withheld from public view.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that limited partnerships in New Zealand confer limited liability while allowing the partners' address details to be withheld from the public register, unlike companies under the Companies Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the public register content required by the Limited Partnerships Act 2008 with s 214 of the Companies Act 1993 and the Companies Office register as at March 2024; true if limited partnerships' address details are withheld from public view while company directors' residential addresses are published, false if both registers publish equivalent address information.

veracity.statement: We want to make sure that small-business owners, who make up the majority of business owners in New Zealand, have the ability to enjoy the same kinds of protections that their big-business - owning counterparts have.
veracity.explanation: Contains a factual claim embedded in the aspiration: that small-business owners constitute the majority of business owners in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics for the year referenced; true if small enterprises (conventionally those with fewer than 20 employees) account for more than half of New Zealand enterprises or their owners, false if they do not.

rigor.statement: If Labour and ACT can agree, surely we can agree that this is, indeed, sticking up for the little guy.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to consensus: the offered reason to support the bill is that two normally-opposed parties agree on it, not anything about what the bill does. Cross-party agreement is not evidence that a measure is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I hope members in all parties can listen to this debate and change their minds here and now, because there is nothing in this bill which would create harm, there is nothing in this bill which would put the directors in a worse position than they were before, and there’s certainly nothing in this bill that would put shareholders in a worse position than they were before.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (members should switch their votes) rests on a bare tripled assertion of no harm, with nothing offered to establish it — an argument from absence of evidence that also leaves the evasion risk raised earlier in the debate unaddressed. Repeating a premise three times is not support for it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But there’s no reason why that review of the Companies Act can’t go ahead at the same time as this provision would come in.
rigor.explanation: A valid rebuttal that engages the Minister's stated reason for delay: a broader review and an interim provision are not mutually exclusive, so the review does not by itself justify voting the bill down. Marked down only because nothing is offered to show the two would not conflict.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So the news today of the official cash rate dropping another 50 basis points and decreasing mortgage rates is welcome news for families struggling with mortgage repayments, but it is also welcome news for our growers, farmers, and businesses across Hawke’s Bay because it gives confidence and certainty and more money to invest in growing our economy and creating jobs, and this lifts wages for everyone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Reserve Bank cut the official cash rate by 50 basis points on the day of the speech (8 October 2025).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review decision of 8 October 2025; true if the OCR was reduced by 50 basis points on that date, false if the cut was a different size or no cut was made.

veracity.statement: A highlight in the last few weeks was visiting the Hastings Stortford Lodge saleyards, and it was amazing to see the farmer confidence back again, with record highs in farmer confidence because finally they have a Government that is backing them and allowing our farmers to do what they do best, and that is farm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that farmer confidence is currently at record highs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Federated Farmers Farm Confidence Survey and/or Rabobank Rural Confidence Survey readings for 2025; true if a headline confidence measure reached the highest level in the published series, false if it was merely elevated or below an earlier peak.

veracity.statement: For years, I sat on the board of New Zealand Apples and Pears, and under the Labour Government the apple industry could never meet the $1 billion export mark.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual apple (and pear) export earnings never reached $1 billion at any point during the Labour-led Government of October 2017 to November 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ merchandise trade data and New Zealand Apples & Pears annual export figures for each year 2017/18 through 2022/23; true if no year reached $1 billion, false if any year did.

veracity.statement: In fact, our horticulture exports have hit record highs: $8.5 billion this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that horticulture export revenue reached a record $8.5 billion in the current year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries horticulture export revenue for the year to June 2025; true if the figure is approximately $8.5 billion and is the highest in the series, false if materially different or not a record.

veracity.statement: Around 360,000 Kiwis are employed in our food and fibre sector, about 15 percent of the total workforce.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a headcount of roughly 360,000 people employed in the food and fibre sector and that this is about 15 percent of the total New Zealand workforce.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries employment estimate for the food and fibre sector, divided by Stats NZ HLFS total employment for the same period; true if the headcount is near 360,000 and the share is near 15 percent, false if the share is materially lower (e.g. around 12–13 percent).

veracity.statement: They have used the Investment Boost package of this Government, which enabled a 20 percent tax deduction along with depreciation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Investment Boost policy provides a 20 percent tax deduction on qualifying assets in addition to depreciation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 Investment Boost policy documents and Inland Revenue guidance; true if the scheme allows a 20 percent immediate deduction of a new asset's cost with normal depreciation on the remaining 80 percent, false if the rate or the interaction with depreciation differs.

rigor.statement: A highlight in the last few weeks was visiting the Hastings Stortford Lodge saleyards, and it was amazing to see the farmer confidence back again, with record highs in farmer confidence because finally they have a Government that is backing them and allowing our farmers to do what they do best, and that is farm.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning built on a single site visit: high farmer confidence is attributed causally to the speaker's own Government, with nothing offered to connect the two beyond the coincidence of timing and one anecdotal impression.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I love these stories. We need to keep creating jobs and opportunities, which is done by supporting our primary sector.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a single conversation with one worker in one packhouse is the whole of the support offered for the general conclusion that job creation is achieved by supporting the primary sector.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve slashed the red tape, we’ve got rid of the bureaucracy, and we’ve been out in the world hustling for trade deals so we have better markets to send our good products to, and, wow, is that making a difference.
specificity.explanation: A record claim carrying no checkable content: no regulation, agency, trade agreement or figure is named, so nothing here could be verified or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Cattle were going out the gate for $3,500 each, and this is just phenomenal for the growth of our economy because it motivates more spending and puts more money back into the pockets of New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete per-head price at a named saleyard, though the economic consequence attached to it is asserted in general terms with no quantity or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Around 360,000 Kiwis are employed in our food and fibre sector, about 15 percent of the total workforce.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, directly checkable figures: an employment headcount and its share of the workforce.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They have used the Investment Boost package of this Government, which enabled a 20 percent tax deduction along with depreciation.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific policy and states the mechanism and the rate, so a reader could look up and check the treatment described.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In Hawke’s Bay alone, our region is set to add another thousand new jobs in agriculture and horticulture.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an increase of about one thousand agriculture and horticulture jobs in the Hawke's Bay region; no timeframe is stated by the speaker.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Employment Data (filled jobs) for agriculture and horticulture in the Hawke's Bay region; true if the count rises by roughly 1,000 or more above the 2025 baseline, false if it is flat or falls.

civility.statement: Much better than languishing on welfare.
civility.explanation: A sneering characterisation of people receiving a benefit as 'languishing'. No individual is attacked, so this is short of a personal insult, but it is a disparaging aside about a group rather than an engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are also still concerns from survivors over new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28, and the use of force that is still permitted in care settings.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly — a named clause of the bill and the substantive effect it has (permitted use of force in care settings). No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: However, disabled people have been very clear that the proposed definition risks framing them through a lens of deficit and dependency rather than recognising autonomy, agency, and mana.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a drafting question in the bill — how the definition of "vulnerable adult" frames the people it covers. Entirely policy-directed, with no reference to the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is that bench saying about the level of recognition that violence deserves? I leave that on the Hansard for that side of the House to have to live up to for decades—well, for ever now. It’s on the record. That’s what that side of the House has called for.
focus.explanation: The bill is before the House, so there was policy to engage with, but this passage is about the other side's conduct in the debate and what it says about them — no measure, figure, clause or outcome is named. It attacks a bench rather than a person, so Civility is untouched; this is the tribalism residue Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side of the House and how their speech landed. No clause, cost, mechanism or outcome of the bill is named, so once the characterisation of opponents is removed nothing about the policy remains.

specificity.statement: There are also still concerns from survivors over new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28, and the use of force that is still permitted in care settings.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28) and the practice at issue. Someone could go to the bill and check it. Falls short of 1.0 only because the scale of the concern is not quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise, checkable ratio (28 of 138) against a named body of recommendations. The follow-on call to move faster is unquantified, which keeps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of implementation progress against the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's recommendations: that of 138 recommendations, only 28 are complete or have had progress initiated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown Response Office / Government implementation reporting against the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia) recommendations, as at October 2025. True if the total is 138 recommendations and the number recorded as completed or with progress initiated is 28 (or rounds to it); false if either the denominator or the progress count differs materially.

rigor.statement: By not recognising their harm and by minimising their harm, that is not the State taking accountability for its own violence; that is the State choosing to discriminate about who worthy survivors of violence are, and who deserves to have their violence recognised.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: from the premise that the redress scheme pays only some survivors, to the conclusion that the State is discriminating between worthy and unworthy survivors. The step is arguable but incomplete — a tiered scheme could rest on evidentiary or categorical thresholds rather than a judgement about whose harm counts, and that alternative is not addressed. Judged on the reasoning only; whether the redress bill in fact creates such a hierarchy is a separate factual question.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the preceding speech as "rubbish" that has been "spouted" — mockery and contemptuous dismissal rather than engagement with what was said. Short of a direct personal insult, but under the re-anchored scale this is a genuine civility failure, not merely robust debate.
civility.subject: speaker
